{{Short description|British sociologist (born 1974)}}
{{Use dmy dates|date=February 2024}}
'''Richard Twine''' (born 1974) is a British [[sociologist]] whose research addresses [[environmental sociology]] as well as [[gender studies|gender]], [[animal studies|human/animal]] and [[science studies]].<ref name="TVS"/> He is noted for his "foundational" work in [[critical animal studies]],<ref name="Nocella et al"/> as well as his contributions to [[ecofeminism]]. His work includes developing [[Barbara Noske]]'s notion of the [[animal-industrial complex]] and theorizing the "vegan killjoy", building on [[Sara Ahmed]]'s "feminist killjoy".

Twine is a [[Reader (academia)|reader]] in sociology in the Department of History, Geography & Social Sciences at [[Edge Hill University]], where he is the co-director of the Centre for Human-Animal Studies. He is also the [[chairperson|chair]] of the Research Advisory Committee of [[The Vegan Society]].<ref name="TVS"/><ref name="Sydney interview"/> He is the author of 2010's ''Animals as Biotechnology'' and 2024's ''The Climate Crisis and Other Animals'', as well as a co-editor of 2014's ''The Rise of Critical Animal Studies'' and 2024's ''Violence and Harm in the Animal Industrial Complex''.

==Career==
Twine studied for a [[Bachelor of Arts]] in Sociology and Psychology at the [[University of Stirling]], graduating in 1995, and then went on to study for a [[Master of Arts]] in Sociology at the [[University of Essex]], which he completed in 1996. He was awarded his [[PhD]] in Sociology from [[Manchester Metropolitan University]] in 2002.<ref name="Edge Hill"/> His [[doctoral thesis|thesis]], supervised by [[Gail Hawkes]] and [[Sue Scott (sociologist)|Sue Scott]] and examined by [[Anne Witz]], was entitled ''Ecofeminism and the 'New' Sociologies - A Collaboration Against Dualism''.<ref name="Publications"/>

After completing his studies, Twine spent a decade at [[Lancaster University]], where he was based within the [[ESRC]] Centre for Economic and Social Aspects of Genomics.<ref name="TVS"/> While at Lancaster, he published ''Animals as Biotechnology: Ethics, Sustainability and Critical Animal Studies'' as part of the [[Earthscan]] Science in Society Series.<ref name="Animals as Biotechnology"/> This was "the first book fully dedicated to" [[critical animal studies]].<ref name="Nocella et al"/> It offered, in the words of one reviewer, "an impressive analysis of the biotech and meat industries from an unapologetically pro-animal perspective".<ref>{{cite journal|author=Lynch, Joseph J.|year=2012|title=Animals as Biotechnology: Ethics, Sustainability and Critical Animal Studies|journal=[[Journal of Animal Ethics]]|volume=2|issue=2|pages=232–4|doi=10.5406/janimalethics.2.2.0232}}</ref> In 2012, he published an article in the ''Journal for Critical Animal Studies'', developing [[Barbara Noske]]'s idea of the [[animal-industrial complex]] as [[research method]] and concept central to critical animal studies.<ref>Twine, Richard (2012). "[https://www.criticalanimalstudies.org/wp-content/uploads/2012/10/JCAS+Volume+10+Issue+1+2012+FINAL.pdf#page=13 Revealing the 'Animal-Industrial Complex' – A Concept & Method for Critical Animal Studies?]" ''Journal for Critical Animal Studies'' 10 (1): 12-39.</ref>

After finishing at Lancaster, Twine worked briefly at the [[University of Glasgow]]<ref name="Contributors"/> and the [[UCL Institute of Education]].<ref name="TVS"/> He published the [[edited collection|collection]] ''The Rise of Critical Animal Studies: From the Margins to the Centre'', co-edited with [[Nik Taylor]], with [[Routledge]] in 2014.<ref name="Rise"/> The same year, he joined [[Edge Hill University]].<ref name="ORCID"/> He also published a paper in ''[[Societies (journal)|Societies]]''<ref name="Societies"/> in which he drew upon [[Sara Ahmed]]'s notion of a [[feminist killjoy]], coining the idea of a "vegan killjoy".<ref name="Killjoy"/> Twine argues that, in a culture in which meat-eating is the norm, a vegan can, by their mere presence, challenge [[anthropocentrism|anthropocentric]] attitudes and practices, affecting the enjoyment that others have in eating animal products.<ref name="Societies"/> This, Twine claims, can serve as "critical deconstructive work".<ref name="Societies"/> The idea of the vegan killjoy has been widely deployed in [[vegan studies]] and related fields.<ref name="Killjoy"/> His book ''The Climate Crisis and Other Animals'', published by [[Sydney University Press]],<ref name="Sydney interview">{{cite web|url=https://sydneyuniversitypress.com/blogs/news/q-a-with-richard-twine-author-of-the-climate-crisis-and-other-animals|title=Q&A with Richard Twine, Author of The Climate Crisis and Other Animals|publisher=[[Sydney University Press]]|date=3 April 2024|accessdate=22 April 2024}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal|author=Johnson, A. M.|year=2025|title=The Climate Crisis and Other Animals|journal=Anthrozoös|doi=10.1080/08927936.2025.2476292}}</ref> and his co-edited collection ''Violence and Harm in the Animal Industrial Complex: Human-Animal Entanglements''<ref>https://www.routledge.com/Violence-and-Harm-in-the-Animal-Industrial-Complex-Human-Animal-Entanglements/Hunnicutt-Twine-Mentor/p/book/9781032579788</ref> were both released in 2024.

{{As of|2024}}, Twine is a [[Reader (academia)|reader]] in sociology in the Department of History, Geography & Social Sciences at Edge Hill<ref name="Edge Hill"/> and co-director of the university's Centre for Human-Animal Studies.<ref name="Sydney interview"/>

==Selected publications==
*Twine, Richard (2010). ''Animals as Biotechnology: Ethics, Sustainability and Critical Animal Studies''. London: Earthscan.
*Twine, Richard (2010). "Intersectional disgust? Animals and (eco)feminism". ''[[Feminism & Psychology]]'' 20 (3): 397–406. {{doi|10.1177/0959353510368284}}.
*Twine, Richard (2012). "[https://www.criticalanimalstudies.org/wp-content/uploads/2012/10/JCAS+Volume+10+Issue+1+2012+FINAL.pdf#page=13 Revealing the 'Animal-Industrial Complex' – A Concept & Method for Critical Animal Studies?]" ''Journal for Critical Animal Studies'' 10 (1): 12–39.
*Twine, Richard (2014). "[https://www.mdpi.com/2075-4698/4/4/623 Vegan Killjoys at the Table—Contesting Happiness and Negotiating Relationships with Food Practices]". ''[[Societies (journal)|Societies]]'' 4 (4): 623–39. {{doi|10.3390/soc4040623|doi-access=free}}.
*Taylor, Nik, and Richard Twine, eds. (2014). ''The Rise of Critical Animal Studies: From the Margins to the Centre''. London: Routledge.
*Twine, Richard (2017). "Materially Constituting a Sustainable Food Transition: The Case of Vegan Eating Practice". ''[[Sociology (journal)|Sociology]]'' 52 (1): 166–81. {{doi|10.1177/0038038517726647}}.
*Twine, Richard (2024). ''The Climate Crisis and Other Animals''. Sydney: Sydney University Press.
*Hunnicutt, Gwen, Richard Twine, and Kenneth Mentor, eds. (2024). ''Violence and Harm in the Animal Industrial Complex: Human-Animal Entanglements''. Abingdon: Routledge.
